memory_leads.lead: Shipboard safety management is a chain of distinct roles rather than one compliance owner: owner/operator or defined shore company, ship manager, designated shore safety interface, master, officers and crew, departmental or safety functions, internal/external auditors and flag/class/port oversight can observe or act on different parts of the same safety state.

A safety-management policy or procedure is a controlled instruction state, not proof that work was performed safely. Issue/revision, distribution or availability, onboard understanding, task execution and later verification can diverge in time; exact SMS manuals and code clauses remain source-specific.

Operational risk assessment is remembered as a pre-task and change-sensitive state chain: identify task/hazard, consider exposure and controls, authorize or accept a controlled plan, execute, monitor changed conditions and review afterward. Exact matrices, scores and approval thresholds require Evidence.

Permit-to-work and toolbox/pre-job controls form a bounded authorization workflow for higher-risk or unusual work: scope, responsible persons, isolation or other prerequisites, simultaneous-operation conflicts, briefing, permit validity, suspension/revalidation and closure are separate states rather than one signed form.

Drills, exercises and familiarization have their own trajectory: requirement or plan, scheduling, participation, scenario execution, observation, debrief, identified improvement and follow-up action. Completion of a drill does not by itself establish operational competence or future emergency performance.

Hazard observation, unsafe condition and near-miss reporting should remain distinct from actual incident occurrence. A report can enter an investigation or corrective-action queue without proving that harm occurred, while the absence of reports is not proof that hazards were absent.

Incident handling separates immediate control from later truth finding: make-safe/emergency response, notification, evidence preservation, preliminary reporting, investigation, causal analysis, corrective action and external review can occur on different clocks. Later findings must not be backfilled into the contemporaneous operational state.

Safety-management findings create an open-item lifecycle. Observation, deficiency or nonconformity labels can vary by regime and scope, but structurally an issue can be recorded, assigned, given a due state, temporarily controlled, corrected, verified for effectiveness and only then closed; exact classifications remain Evidence work.

Corrective and preventive action are not the same as writing an action plan. Root-cause or contributing-factor hypotheses, chosen action, responsibility, target date, implementation, evidence of completion, effectiveness review and recurrence monitoring can diverge; unresolved actions form a safety backlog.

Internal audit, external audit/certification, class or flag attendance and port-state-type inspection are different observation channels with different scope and authority. Their findings should preserve who observed what, when and under which scope rather than collapsing them into one vessel-compliance truth flag.

Management review and master's/onboard review form a feedback layer above individual actions: recurring incidents or near misses, audit findings, overdue actions, training or maintenance issues and procedural weaknesses can be aggregated into priorities, resource decisions and revised controls without converting management opinion into verified causation.

Safety-management backlog can propagate into operations through temporary controls, task restrictions, additional supervision, maintenance work, training, revised procedures or delayed work. The existence of an open action does not automatically mean the vessel is unfit or off-hire, but repeated unresolved high-consequence items can increase operational risk.

Shore instructions and shipboard command authority should be stored as an interaction, not a single hierarchy bit. The master and onboard team may need to adapt, suspend or escalate work when actual conditions differ from the plan, while shore management supplies policy, resources and review; exact legal authority boundaries remain jurisdiction- and contract-specific.

P057 technical-management memory is refined because defect and maintenance closure can require a parallel safety-control state: isolation, risk assessment, work authorization, temporary operating controls and verification may remain open even after the physical repair is nominally complete.

P059 crewing memory is refined because certificates, medicals and training readiness do not themselves establish safe task execution; familiarization, briefing, watch/team coordination, fatigue context and compliance with live controls remain separate operational states.

P054 casualty memory is refined by preserving the pre-casualty safety-management record and later investigation as separate timelines. A later causal finding may explain an earlier gap, but it must not rewrite what the crew or shore organization actually knew before the event.

P053 survey/inspection memory is refined because audit or inspection findings are scoped observations with downstream action states; a finding can trigger remediation or restriction without becoming self-executing proof of overall compliance, competence or causation.

P054 already covers immediate casualty response, notifications, investigation and later cause/fault separation. P060 reuses that boundary while adding the routine safety-management and corrective-action layer that exists before and after incidents.

P053 already establishes that inspection and survey output is a scoped timestamped observation rather than self-executing truth. P060 applies the same epistemic separation to audits, near-miss reports and safety findings rather than creating a second observation semantics.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Operational control content and legal/regulatory requirements vary by company, vessel, task, regime and rule vintage and require authoritative Evidence.
Event records, competence conclusions and causation findings are claim-scoped Evidence and should not be inferred from structural Memory.
Finding taxonomy, certification effect, required response and closure are scope- and authority-specific facts.
Provider identity, current capability and comparative safety performance are source-first questions outside blind Memory.

stop_reason: The shipboard safety-management layer is populated from role separation and controlled procedures through risk assessment, permit/toolbox authorization, drills/familiarization, hazard/near-miss reporting, incident handling, finding/open-item state, corrective action, verification, audit and management review. Further recall becomes procedure-, matrix-, permit-, drill-, incident-, finding-, certification-, provider- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation and not safety, regulatory, class, audit, legal, operational or casualty advice; no SMS procedure, risk score, permit validity, drill result, incident or near-miss fact, nonconformity, corrective action, audit/certification status, compliance conclusion, provider capability or causal finding is verified.
